title: Pendle redemption passes a deliberately slack minimum to the router while enforcing the caller's strict minimum on the measured balance delta
content:
Two different minimums appear in the same procedure. A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.11.3 computes the one handed to Pendle:

```
uint256 minTokenOut = params.pyAmountIn * 1e18 / pyIndexCurrent - 5;
```

and states the reason for the constant: "A rounding buffer of `5` is subtracted from `minTokenOut` to avoid reverts caused by potential rounding errors." A...11.1.6 then applies the real test after the call, against measured state:

```
uint256 totalTokenOutAmount = IERC20(tokenOut).balanceOf(proxy) - tokenOutAmountBefore;
require(totalTokenOutAmount >= params.minAmountOut, "PendleLib/min-amount-not-met");
```

The division of labour matters. The router-facing minimum only needs to catch gross failure, and making it exact would let a one-wei truncation revert an otherwise correct redemption — so it is loosened by a fixed epsilon. The caller-facing minimum is where Grove's actual tolerance lives, it is checked on a balance the proxy owns, and it cannot be zero (`min-amount-out-not-set`, A...11.1.2).

The general lesson is that a protocol-facing guard and a policy guard should not be the same number. Conflating them forces a choice between spurious reverts and weak protection; separating them gets both.
description: minTokenOut is derived from the PY index minus a hardcoded rounding buffer of 5 wei; the authoritative check is a separate require on the proxy's actual tokenOut increase.
